signals.excerpt:
# PyTorch Conference 2026: Google and Meta Open-Source TorchTPU for Native PyTorch on TPUs 

Oct 25, 2026 4 min read 

by

- Andrew Hoblitzell 

At PyTorch Conference North America 2026 in San Jose, Google and Meta open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). Meta, which created PyTorch in 2016, plans to move larger-scale LLM workloads onto TPUs with it, Meta software engineer Zongwei Zhou said in the October 21 keynotes.

TorchTPU replaces PyTorch/XLA, a lazy-tensor bridge from 2020 that, according to the announcement, "required intrusive source-code modifications." The new backend aims to make porting a model as simple as changing `model.to("cuda")` to `model.to("tpu")`. "With TorchTPU, TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch," Google Cloud wrote in its announcement, co-authored by Bill Jia, VP of engineering for Core ML/AI.

...

Because TorchTPU plugs into PyTorch's low-level dispatcher, the speakers said, Hugging Face models worked with it out of the box. The vLLM and SGLang inference engines run natively, and TorchTitan supports dense, mixture-of-experts, and diffusion models for training at scale. Ray and llm-d scale TPU workloads across hosts on Kubernetes. Four repositories were open sourced: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, and TorchTitan.

Jia showed near-linear scaling past 8,000 TPU chips, with per-chip throughput holding roughly constant as the cluster grew. Google's published results include a Qwen3 235B mixture-of-experts run on 8,192 TPU v7x chips at 28% model FLOPs utilization. The announcement is candid that the one-line change is only a starting point:

> One cannot achieve peak TPU performance with that simple change, since a model's shapes, sharding and ops may be skewed toward a GPU architecture; however, the model should run out of the box.

signals.title: Introducing Infinity: a runtime for extreme agent concurrency | AWS Open Source Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Introducing Infinity: a runtime for extreme agent concurrency

by Shadaj Laddad on 23 OCT 2026 in Announcements Permalink Share

Agents spend much of their time waiting on tools. A coding agent may start a build that runs for twenty minutes, a triage agent may wait hours for the next pull request on a repository, and an assistant may wait until the next morning for an approval. Most agent harnesses run the agent loop as a sequence of blocking steps: the harness calls the model, invokes a tool, waits for the tool to return, and repeats. While the agent waits, it holds a process and its memory, and it cannot respond to events that arrive in the meantime.

Today, we’re releasing Infinity under the Apache 2.0 open source license as part of the Hydro project, a collaborative effort between AWS and UC Berkeley. Infinity is a research project that re-imagines agent runtimes, based on the techniques that programming languages use to suspend and resume asynchronous functions. When an agent calls a tool, Infinity dispatches the call, saves the conversation, and suspends the agent. When the tool result arrives, the runtime resumes the agent from its saved state.

signals.title: Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Deploying a trained neural network involves more than translating each operator into a GPU kernel. It is a compilation problem with many legitimate answers. For example, when NVIDIA TensorRT builds an engine, it makes interdependent decisions about graph-IR transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. This process is called scheduling. Different scheduling choices can preserve model semantics yet produce very different inference performance, making scheduling central to deep learning compiler optimization.

No single scheduling strategy is best for every model and deployment environment. A transformation that accelerates one network may slow another. A kernel that is faster in isolation may interact poorly with fusion, tensor layouts, or memory traffic elsewhere in the graph. Aggressive scheduling may improve performance while violating an application’s accuracy requirement. These coupled, model-dependent effects often appear only after the complete engine is built and measured, making the right strategy increasingly difficult to predict.

This post is Part 1 of a two-part series that is intended to develop a clearer way of reasoning about performance optimization. It explores questions such as: What makes one compiled engine better than another? Why can individually promising decisions fail end to end? How should accuracy constrain performance optimization? It introduces the Global Performance Tuner, a feature for automatic performance tuning released in TensorRT 11.1, and explores these questions through an intuitive example and mathematical framework.

# MiniMax releases open weights for 428-billion-parameter M3.1 Flash model 

 by TechNode Feed Oct 23, 2026 

MiniMax released the weights for its M3.1 Flash model on October 23, making the model available for developers to download and deploy. The mixture-of-experts model has approximately 428 billion total parameters, with 23 billion activated per token. It supports text, image and video inputs and a context window of up to 1 million tokens.

Designed for coding, AI agents and computer-use tasks, M3.1 Flash improves inference efficiency through sparse attention, quantization-aware training and speculative decoding. The release includes deployment guidance for inference frameworks such as SGLang and vLLM, alongside support for multiple chip platforms through FlagOS. The weights follow the model’s initial service launch on October 19. [MiniMax]

## Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have transformed knowledge discovery, but their use in sensitive domains is limited by privacy concerns and risks of data leakage. Moreover, LLMs may hallucinate when queried about information outside their training data, undermining their reliability for scientific, clinical, or policy-related tasks. We present MyGPT, a fully open-source, privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) platform that uses open-source LLMs and operates locally or within secure institutional environments. MyGPT empowers users to query user-defined libraries such as biomedical literature, confidential clinical documents, and multilingual global health policies, while ensuring that sensitive data never leaves the secure environment. We introduce confidence metrics, including “relevance scores” and “hallucination index,” and provide explicit source citation from the library within a single interface to assess contextual support for generated answers. MyGPT offers a cost-effective, modular, open-source alternative to commercial LLM services and democratizes knowledge-seeking across multiple domains, including use at remote facilities without internet access.

signals.title: Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
signals.excerpt:
Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
* Article
* Open access
* Published: 26 October 2026
# Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs
* Enmiao Feng 1,
* Gaike Wang 2,
* Pengfei Li 1,
* Yinuo Wang ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0004-3927-0742 3 &
* …
* Shan Huang 4
## Abstract
Large language model (LLM) inference workloads are bursty, have output lengths that are unknown at arrival, expose two resource-distinct phases (prefill and decode), and serve requests carrying heterogeneous service-level objectives (SLOs) on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). Prevailing schedulers rely on static heuristics that cannot adapt to this uncertainty, while online reinforcement learning (RL) is unsafe and sample-inefficient in production. We present URSA, an uncertainty-aware, risk-sensitive scheduler trained *entirely offline*, without interacting with a live serving system, on scheduling transitions generated by replaying historical request traces under existing heuristic schedulers. URSA (i) predicts a calibrated *distribution* over each request’s output length and derived key–value (KV) cache footprint rather than a point estimate; (ii) encodes the joint state of the waiting queue, heterogeneous GPU instances, and KV occupancy as a request–instance heterogeneous graph processed by a graph neural network; (iii) learns a dispatch policy with conservative, distributional offline RL whose reward jointly optimizes SLO attainment, goodput, and KV-overflow risk; and (iv) reserves memory at a class-dependent high quantile of the predicted footprint to bound out-of-memory events. Across the BurstGPT, Azure LLM inference, and Alibaba GPU-cluster traces, URSA raises overall SLO attainment from \\(71.3\\%\\) (FCFS) and \\(84.1\\%\\) (learning-to-rank) to \\(90.4\\%\\), cuts P99 TTFT by up to \\(3.3\\times \\), and reduces recompute/eviction events below \\(1\\%\\), approaching an oracle that knows true lengths. We analyze limitations, robustness to prediction error, and transfer to other scheduling domains.

# Meta Releases Wonder, Opens Spark All about Muse Wonder (API), Muse Wonder Full (subscription), and Muse Spark Open (weights available)

Published Oct 23, 2026

Meta marched all the way back to the AI frontier to offer a Muse model for everyone: a high-end agentic model (comparable to Claude Sonnet 5.5) that costs $50 per month to access, its moderately-priced sibling (comparable to GPT-6.1 Sol), and an open model that outperforms any yet released by a company outside China.

What’s new: Meta made three multimodal models available in one week, including the top-of-the-line Muse Wonder Full, the multimodal Muse Wonder, and the locally deployable Muse Spark Open. Muse Wonder is available via API and Muse Spark Open’s weights are free to download, but Muse Wonder Full is only available to Muse Code subscribers.

- Input/output: Text, image, video, and audio in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (up to 128,000 tokens), 139 tokens/second (Muse Wonder) and 143 tokens/second (Muse Spark Open)
- Architecture: Mixture-of-experts transformer, 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active per token, 256 experts (Muse Spark Open)
- Features: Six reasoning levels (minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max), reasoning always on, tool calling, structured outputs
- Performance: Tied for second on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index (56, Muse Wonder Full); seventh (52, Muse Wonder); seventh among open weight models, first among U.S. open models (39, Muse Spark Open)
- Availability: API and subscription (Muse Wonder), subscription only (Muse Wonder Full), weights available via Meta and Hugging Face (Muse Spark Open)
- Price: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens (Muse Wonder); $50/month (Muse Wonder Full); $1.25/$4.15 input/output (Muse Spark Open)
- Weights/license: Weights for Muse Spark Open available under the Muse Model license, which allows for commercial and noncommercial use for up to $20 million of revenue; display of “Built with Muse Spark Open” required for products and services using the model; separate licenses available for other users; Muse Wonder and Wonder Full are proprietary
- Undisclosed: Knowledge cutoff, parameters and architecture for Muse Wonder models, specific training datasets and methods

...

How it works: Meta released a model card for Muse Wonder and Wonder Full, but it reveals very little about the model’s architecture or how it was trained.

Performance: Muse Wonder Full is the top-performing of the three models, two points behind Claude Opus 5.5 and identical with Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index. Muse Spark Open is the top open weights model outside China, ahead of Mistral Large 4 and Reflection’s Beam. Its Intelligence Index average is identical with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash’s, but is still behind MiMo-V.2.6-Pro’s and GLM-5.3’s.

- On AA’s Intelligence Index, a weighted average of ten independent benchmarks, Muse Wonder Full achieved a 56, Muse Wonder a 52, and Muse Spark Open a 39. Meta’s former flagship model, Muse Spark 1.3, achieved an average of 48.
- Muse Wonder costs $4.52 per Intelligence Index task, fifth highest among current models; Wonder Full’s cost per task cannot be measured, since it’s not available via API. Muse Spark Open costs $0.84 per task, more than GPT-6.1 Sol, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. 
- Artificial Analysis notes Muse Wonder and Wonder Full’s low knowledge marks but also partly offset this through their low hallucination rates. On the AA-Omniscience Index, Muse Wonder Full (30) and Wonder (25) place 8th and 10th respectively.
- Muse Spark Open only requires about 1 TB of memory at 4-bit precision. This means it can be run locally on 2 Mac Studios with 512 GB of memory each (or 4 with 256 GB, etc.). Meta and Apple touted their work together to make the model capable of running on Apple’s consumer-grade silicon.

README

# forge

PyPI
Tests
codecov
Python 3.12+
License: MIT

A reliability layer for self-hosted LLM tool-calling. You give forge a set of tools; the model calls whichever it wants in whatever order. Workflow structure is opt-in — `required_steps`, `prerequisites`, and `terminal_tool` let you constrain the loop when you need to, but forge's guardrails (rescue parsing, retry nudges, response validation) apply with zero required steps too.

Forge takes an 8B local model from single digits to 84% across forge's 26-scenario v0.7.0 eval suite — and even lifts Sonnet 4.6 from 85% to 98% on the same workload (Anthropic numbers measured in v0.6.0; not re-run in v0.7.0 since the cost is non-trivial).

**What forge isn't:**
- **Not an agent orchestrator.** Forge sits inside one agentic loop and makes its tool calls reliable. Multi-agent graphs, DAG planners, and cross-agent coordination are out of scope.
- **Not a coding harness.** Forge is domain-agnostic. If you're building a coding agent (or already using one like opencode, aider, Cline), proxy mode lifts your existing harness with forge's guardrails — no rewrite.

**Three ways to use it:**

- **Proxy server** — Drop-in proxy (`forge-proxy` from the standalone distribution, or `python -m forge.proxy` from the Python package) speaking both the OpenAI chat-completions and Anthropic Messages (`/v1/messages`) APIs, sitting between any client and a local model server. Point OpenAI-compatible tools (opencode, Continue, aider) **or Claude Code** at it and forge applies guardrails transparently — the client thinks it's talking to a smarter model. Most popular entry point.

- **WorkflowRunner** — Define tools, pick a backend, run structured agent loops. Forge manages the full lifecycle: system prompts, tool execution, context compaction, and guardrails. **SlotWorker** adds priority-queued access to a shared inference slot with auto-preemption — for multi-agent architectures where specialist workflows share a GPU slot. Best when you're building on forge directly.

- **Guardrails middleware** — Use forge's reliability stack (composable middleware) inside your own orchestration loop. You control the loop; forge validates responses, rescues malformed tool calls, and enforces required steps.

Supports generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Ollama, llama-server (llama.cpp),
Llamafile, vLLM, and Anthropic as backends.

## Distributed AI inference grows up with llm-d v1.0 release

On Tuesday, at PyTorch Conference North America, the CNCF sandbox project llm-d reached v1.0. The project now bridges AI application developers in the PyTorch ecosystem and the production cloud-native stack.

Carlos Costa, co-founder and lead maintainer of llm-d, and a distinguished engineer on IBM’s hybrid cloud platform for AI, says the v1.0 release signals maturity. 

“This is the moment open source AI serving crosses from experimental projects into dependable infrastructure you can build on,” Costa tells The New Stack. Whereas earlier versions focused on proving state-of-the-art performance, v1.0 is about sustaining that performance in production, he adds.

llm-d has already seen plenty of use at Tesla, AWS, Oracle, Google, and beyond. Costa adds that a recent IBM Research demonstration found that an agent factory exploring quantum error correction hardware ran at 11.5x lower inference cost on open models with llm-d than on an all-proprietary configuration. 

“This demonstration shows where llm-d really shines: agentic workloads,” he says, adding that it absorbs bursty agentic traffic and, in IBM’s test, pushed cache reuse to about 98%.

signals.excerpt:
Google has released ML Drift, an open-source, cross-platform GPU compute engine designed for on-device AI and machine learning inference. Licensed under Apache 2.0, it abstracts the complexities of different GPU hardware and low-level APIs, supporting OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU.

ML Drift is the core GPU acceleration engine that powers LiteRT. By open-sourcing it, Google is enabling developers to build custom graphics and inference runtimes for applications ranging from traditional computer vision, audio, and depth processing to generative AI.

One of ML Drift's main goal is simplifying access to the diverse GPU hardware that developers encounter when creating applications for edge devices.

...

To achieve this, ML Drift introduces several technical improvements over the legacy TFLite GPU delegate, including unified shaders through tensor virtualization, extensible custom operations, and five-dimensional tensor support. It also incorporates hardware-specific optimizations for GPUs from Arm, Intel, and Qualcomm Technologies to "maximize hardware utilization across modern GPUs".

ML Drift extends desktop support for inference on Windows and Linux through Dawn, Chromium's WebGPU implementation, while retaining native Metal backend support on macOS. Dawn provides a unified API model leveraging WebGPU's hardware abstraction layer, avoiding the need to interface directly with platform-specific graphics APIs such as DirectX and Vulkan.

signals.title: AMD Adds MiniMax-M3.1 Support for Instinct MI350 Series GPUs | TokenPost
signals.excerpt:
# AMD Adds MiniMax-M3.1 Support for Instinct MI350 Series GPUs

The ROCm update supports vLLM and ATOM. AMD measured lower decode latency and higher interactivity in selected tests.

By Simon Yoon

Published Oct 23, 2026, 5:57 PM EDT

A black accelerator module rests on a vivid red platform / TokenPost.ai

AMD announced Thursday, Oct. 22, that MiniMax-M3.1 can run on Instinct MI350 Series GPUs through ROCm versions of vLLM and ATOM, bringing a coding and agent model with a context window of one million tokens to AMD’s inference stack.

MiniMax-M3.1 includes reasoning and tool-use features. AMD’s setup supports the original NVFP4 checkpoint after conversion during loading, as well as an MXFP4 export made with AMD Quark. The ATOM configuration AMD tested uses the Quark export. AITER kernels handle expert routing, attention and reduction operations. AMD said the two weight paths performed within evaluation error of each other on GSM8K, AIME and MMMU-Pro.

ATOM applies per-channel FP8 attention and combines shared-expert work during startup. It also uses CUDA graphs to capture DSpark’s draft pass; AMD’s tests found that roughly half of DSpark’s seven-token draft proposals were accepted on real text. The MI350 implementation uses four-way tensor parallelism per replica, allowing two replicas on an eight-GPU node.

In AMD’s tests, vLLM mono decode reduced per-token decode latency by a factor of 3.2 at one request, 2.1 at four and 1.5 at 16, compared with the same server with mono decode disabled. On coding-agent traces, AMD said mono decode produced 2.2x to 2.4x the interactivity across one to eight concurrent users. Pairing it with DSpark speculative decoding increased interactivity by about one-third for one to four users and 13% at eight users in the reported tests.

The current configuration supports mono decode with DSpark for up to four concurrent requests. Wider decode steps use the standard path. AMD listed wider mono-decode steps and support for MiniMax-M3.1 mono decode in ATOM as future work, without a timeline.

signals.title: Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang - MarkTechPost

# Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang

By

Asif Razzaq

October 26, 2026

Tsinghua University and CUHK researchers open-sourced AKV, a serving system for KV cache engineering in LLM agents. Instead of summarizing old history, agents drop selected KV cache entries and keep reusing the rest. Across 3 models and 4 agent benchmarks, average cost falls 27.7%. Average task score rises 1.7 points. The code is Apache-2.0 licensed and builds on SGLang.

...

## What does the AKV API look like?

The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible. Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. `drop_message` maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. `reposition` lists the indices after which positions get compacted.

A `CachePolicy` builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A `CacheTool` lets the model call `drop_context` itself.

signals.title: Hugging Face Publishes 207 WebGPU Kernels for Browser AI | WebGL / WebGPU
signals.excerpt:
# Hugging Face Publishes 207 WebGPU Kernels for Browser AI

Hugging Face has released 207 versioned WebGPU kernels, a JavaScript loader and Fleet benchmarking for local browser AI workloads.

Published

October 25, 2026

On this page More than a folder of shaders

- More than a folder of shaders
- Faster on an Apple M4, with caveats
- Fleet takes testing beyond one GPU

Hugging Face has released (opens in a new tab) an initial collection of 207 open-source WebGPU kernels for local AI workloads, accompanied by a JavaScript library that downloads and runs them directly from the Hugging Face Hub. Announced by Nico Martin (opens in a new tab) and Joshua Lochner (opens in a new tab), the collection covers the low-level operations that browser inference runtimes repeatedly need: matrix multiplication, normalization, convolution, attention primitives, quantization, broadcasting and tensor layout transformations. Everything is Apache 2.0 licensed. This is foundational work rather than another model demo. Faster browser inference ultimately depends on faster individual operations, and WebGPU portability alone does not guarantee good performance across every device.

...

## Faster on an Apple M4, with caveats

Hugging Face compared its kernels against ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU using a development version of ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0. The evaluation started with 1,756 cases across all 207 operations. Hugging Face’s published aggregate covers the 809 cases where both systems produced matching outputs and reliable timings. Across those cases, the company reports a 2.57x geometric-mean speedup and a 1.90x median speedup, with 629 wins, 176 losses and four ties. Familiar operations showed more moderate improvements: Add reached 3.52x, Softmax 2.11x, LayerNormalization 2.22x and MatMul 1.14x. Some specialized workloads produced extreme results. A bilinear `Einsum` case ran more than 10,000 times faster, while a row-wise `CumSum` reported a 301x improvement.

signals.excerpt:
# Recursive releases Flint, an open-weight coding model with about 2.5 billion active parameters

Recursive says its Apache-licensed mixture-of-experts model leads MoE rivals under 50 billion parameters on agentic coding benchmarks; the scores are its own, and a dense Qwen model leads it on four of six.

23 October 2026 Share

Recursive, the start-up behind the "Eureka Machine" automated-research system, has released Flint, an open-weight coding model whose Hugging Face repository was created on 21 October 2026. The model card describes it as "Recursive’s mixture-of-experts language model for coding agents, with 39.8 billion total parameters and approximately 2.5 billion active per token."

...

## The benchmark scores are Recursive's own

The card states: "In our release evaluations, it scores 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 89.7% on SWE-bench Pro v2, and 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified." It adds that "† marks scores measured by Recursive; other comparison scores are developer-reported", and that "Evaluation setups vary across sources." It also says: "Flint’s Terminal-Bench score counts solutions obtained through web retrieval as unsuccessful; developer-reported scores may not apply the same adjustment." The whole SWE-bench Pro v2 panel carries the † mark.

The comparison chart is an image. It has six benchmark panels, each comparing Flint with six other models: three sparse MoE models (Qwen 3.5, Qwen 3.6, Laguna XS 2.1) and three dense models of 27–31 billion parameters (Qwen 3.8, Muse Glimmer, Gemma 4). The card's version adds Flint's NVFP4 checkpoint.

Against the three MoE models, Flint scores highest in five panels. On LiveCodeBench v6, Qwen 3.6's 80.4 edges Flint's 80.3 in BF16; the NVFP4 checkpoint scores 80.8. Against the dense models, rivals lead in four of six panels:

- Terminal-Bench 2.1: Qwen 3.8 73.0, Flint 54.9
- SWE-bench Pro v2: Qwen 3.8 94.9, Flint 89.7
- SWE-bench Verified: Muse Glimmer 76.0 and Qwen 3.8 75.6, Flint 74.2
- LiveCodeBench v6: Qwen 3.8 90.3, Flint 80.3

Flint leads every model shown on IFBench (89.2) and IFEval (95.1). On Recursive's M4 Pro speed chart, Flint's MLX build is faster than every listed rival except the small Qwen 3.5 0.8B at short context, and Qwen 3.5 0.8B and 2B on the long-context average.

We found no independent benchmark evaluation. Artificial Analysis's models page had no Flint listing when we checked on 23 October, and we could not load LMArena's leaderboard. Every score here is the company's own.

# FP4 W/A+FP4 KV的强化学习也能「又快又稳」：阿里千问提出TRACE，Rollout最高加速5.4倍
2026-10-23 20:22:23 来源: 机器之心Pro 天津 举报
大模型强化学习越来越「吃算力」，最昂贵的环节之一正是 Rollout。把 Rollout 从 BF16 压到 FP4，理论上可以显著降低计算和显存开销，但问题也随之而来 —— 训练端与 Rollout 端即使面对非常接近的数值，也可能因为 FP4 的离散量化边界而落到不同码点，最终把微小的数值误差放大成策略偏差导致训练崩溃。
阿里千问联合俄亥俄州立大学的研究团队提出了 TRACE。它的核心思路并不是继续分别提高训练端和 Rollout 端的量化精度，而是直接减少两条低精度执行路径之间的差异：用 Rollout 侧真实的 FP4 量化结果，反过来指导训练侧的舍入方向。在 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B、Qwen3.5-122B-A10B、Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 以及 Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B 四个 MoE 模型上，TRACE 可以在联合 FP4 W/A 与 FP4 KV Cache Rollout 的设置下，将最终性能拉回到 BF16 Rollout 附近，同时在 128K 输出长度下 rollout 获得最高 5.4× 的解码吞吐提升。
* 论文标题：TRACE: Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training for FP4 Reinforcement Learning of MoE Language Models
* ArXiv 链接：https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07767
* Huggingface 链接：https://huggingface.co/papers/2610.07767
为什么 FP4 Rollout 会把 RL 训练「搞崩」？
低精度 Rollout 的吸引力很直接：rollout 阶段通常占据 RL 大量时间，尤其当轨迹长度扩展到数万甚至数十万 token 时，低精度计算和低精度 KV Cache 能显著降低成本。相比 FP8，FP4 更激进，也意味着更大的潜在加速空间。但 FP4 的问题也更尖锐。现有方法通常关注「量化后的值离原始高精度值有多近」，也就是分别降低训练路径和 Rollout 路径的量化误差。TRACE 的作者指出，这并不等价于降低两条路径之间的差异。两个值都可以各自量得很准，却仍然被量化到不同码点。
图 1：微小的 BF16 差异跨过 FP4 舍入边界后，可能被放大成显著的低精度差异。
论文给出了一个直观例子：训练侧激活为 60.24，Rollout 侧为 59.76，两者原本只差 0.48；经过相同的 global scale 和 block scale 后，归一化值分别变成 2.51 和 2.49。因为它们恰好位于舍入边界两侧，一个被量化到 3，一个被量化到 2，最终差异被放大到 24。对 MoE 模型而言，这类偏差尤其棘手：数值变化还可能影响 router 分数和专家选择，使训练策略与生成轨迹对应的策略进一步偏离。实验中，所有的 baseline 方法，包括普通 FP4 QAT、QaRL 和 QUADS 都出现了训练后期奖励与测试分数明显下滑甚至崩溃的现象。
图 2：在 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 上，FP4 QAT/QUADS/QaRL 出现性能下降，TRACE 保持稳定，并逐步和 BF16 持平。
TRACE 核心：
别只管「量得准」
直接让训练侧向 Rollout 的量化结果对齐
TRACE 的第一个设计是 Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training。在 Rollout 阶段，系统记录 FP4 routed expert 激活和 FP4 KV 状态对应的量化结果；到了后续训练阶段，这些信息不再只是「历史数据」，而是直接参与训练侧 fake quantization 的舍入决策。具体来说，对于训练侧某个待量化值，TRACE 仍然只在相邻的两个 FP4 E2M1 码点之间选择，但不再机械使用标准 round-to-nearest （RTN）。它会优先选择距离 Rollout 侧实际码点更近的那个候选值。
图 3：TRACE 总体流程。Rollout 侧保存紧凑量化信息，训练侧加载后用于调整 FP4 舍入。
然而，直接保存完整的 Rollout 量化结果并不便宜。这些信息需要经历 GPU→CPU、CPU 缓存、磁盘写入 / 读取，再在训练时回到 GPU；长轨迹、大 batch 和异步 RL 都会放大存储与通信压力。TRACE 的第二个设计，正是把「需要传什么」压到最少。作者统计发现，超过 99% 的训练 /rollout 量化不一致只相差一个相邻 FP4 codebook entry。既然训练侧自身的激活值已经把候选范围压得很小，那么 Rollout 侧没必要把完整低精度值全部传过去；保留少量 mantissa 信息，加上 scale，通常就足够告诉训练侧应该朝哪个方向舍入。
实验效果
在 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 的 RL 任务上，TRACE 的平均分达到 75.3。作为对照，BF16 Rollout 为 74.9，普通 QAT 为 59.6，QaRL 为 58.6，QUADS 为 68.8。尤其在 HMMT25 上，TRACE 从 QUADS 的 59.0 提升到 70.0。
论文专门测了 Rollout 吞吐和端到端 RL step time。结果显示，如果保存完整指导信息，通信开销确实会严重拖慢 Rollout；而采用紧凑缓存后，TRACE 的吞吐基本贴近原生 FP4 Rollout。在 8K 输入、128K 输出时，解码吞吐相对 BF16 Rollout 最高提升 5.4×。端到端来看，联合 FP4 Rollout 的 RL step time 中 TRACE 仅产生约 7.4% 的额外开销。
一个更有意思的现象：
模型会在 RL 中「适应」FP4
TRACE 的实验里还有一个很值得关注的现象：在训练早期，FP4 执行仍会带来性能损失；但只要 train-rollout discrepancy 被控制住，模型会逐步适应这个低精度执行环境。
图 4：TRACE 的性能适应现象，左图为 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B，右图为 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
在 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 的 HMMT25 曲线上，TRACE 大约在 120 个 RL step 后追上 BF16；在 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 上，类似的「追平」 出现在约 240 step。这意味着低精度并不一定只能被看作训练中的静态噪声。若训练与生成使用的是一致、可学习的低精度环境，策略本身可能通过 RL 更新逐步适应这种数值约束。这一点也体现在最终 FP4 policy 的质量上。如果先用 BF16 Rollout 完成 RL，再做事后量化，Vanilla NVFP4、4over6 和 H-Scale 的平均分分别是 70.4、71.0 和 71.4；而 TRACE 从训练过程中就使用联合 FP4 Rollout，最终 FP4 policy 的平均分达到 75.3。

signals.title: Chinese tech company unveils new AI model based on fully domestic computing power - People's Daily Online
signals.excerpt:
By Zhang Weilan (Global Times) 09:11, October 23, 2026

iFlytek 1024 Global Developer Festival 2026 is held in Beijing on October 22, 2026. Photo: Zhang Weilan/Global Times

Chinese tech company iFlytek released and open-sourced its general-purpose large-language model (LLM), Spark-X2.6, at an industry event in Beijing on Thursday. The new model is an end-cloud integrated LLM that the company said has achieved breakthroughs in coding and agentic capabilities using fully domestic computing infrastructure.

The model, sized at 293-A30B mixture-of-experts architecture (293B total parameters, 30B active per token), supports a context window of 1 million tokens and has been deployed on a domestic 10,000-card inference cluster.

"Spark-X2.6 has taken the lead in breaking through the efficiency bottleneck of long-horizon task training on domestic chips, truly achieving independence and controllability with homegrown computing power," the company's chairperson Liu Qingfeng said at the iFlytek 1024 Global Developer Festival 2026 held in Beijing on Thursday.

The company said that the model has reached performance levels comparable to leading industry systems in multiple technical benchmarks. However, Liu emphasized that the model's real-world deployment performance in actual industrial scenarios — such as state-owned enterprises, education, healthcare and judicial services — outperforms its public benchmark scores.

An industry observer attending the event told the Global Times that the emphasis is shifting away from sheer model size and benchmark competition toward deployment on domestic computing, data security, and real-world usefulness in office, industrial and research settings.

signals.title: KV Cache砍掉99%，单卡吞吐飙6倍，港科CMU联手岩山科技开源新模型 – 量子位
signals.excerpt:
> 允中 发自 凹非寺
> 
> 量子位 | 公众号 QbitAI

谷歌今年的一篇论文，愣是把存储芯片巨头的股价都给整出动静了。

论文里提到， KV Cache至少能压缩6倍。

要知道，大模型推理越来越吃内存，KV Cache又是其中一笔不小的开销。

现在谷歌突然把它压下去这么多，美光等存储芯片巨头的股价随之下跌。

结果才过去几个月，又有人对KV Cache下了更狠的一刀。

这次连压缩都不满足了。

上下文从4K一路涨到256K，KV Cache占用愣是没变。

在256K上下文下，始终固定在72MiB。相比源模型，KV Cache直接减少 99.1%。

更夸张的是，一张80GB显卡同时跑512路长推理，输出吞吐达到12124 tokens/s，是源模型的6.42倍。

而且推理能力也基本保住了，AIME 2024—2026平均一次通过率达到82.9%，而参评的有界状态模型即便做到14B，最好也只有18.8%。

signals.title: Deepseek's latest AI model is smarter than ever, but its low running costs come at a price — uses only one-quarter of the HBM and one-eighth of SSD storage but still battles hallucinations in agentic workloads | Tom's Hardware
signals.excerpt:
Deepseek just upgraded its V4.1 Flash open-weight model to revision 1017. What looks like a mere point revision may actually be a significant step forward in model efficiency. On the product page, Deepseek uses the slogan "wish-driven programming made real," a likely reference to the colloquial "vibe coding," implying the model is a good fit for open-ended tasks with broad descriptions. However, while the model is indeed cheap and scores well, it can be hallucination-prone.

LLMs are roughly divided into two categories: closed commercial efforts from frontier labs, whose models are expensive to run but deliver excellent results, and Chinese open-weight competitors that broadly exchange reliability for a much cheaper running cost, particularly for long-running agentic tasks.

Deepseek V4.1 Flash (DSF) is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 552B total parameters, 16B of which are active during runs. The model is multimodal, accepts both text and images as inputs, and its context window length measures the now-standard 1 million tokens.

According to Deepseek's internal benchmarks, the model slots in neatly between GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5, even beating Anthropic's LLM in task tests. That's already a strong showing, but this latest revision of DSF shines in the performance-per-task base and token efficiency. The upgrade from V4 Flash to V4.1 Flash significantly slashed hardware requirements, with V4.1 using only one-quarter of the HBM and one-eighth of SSD storage for its KV cache compared to its predecessor, spending only 890 bytes per token entry.

...

DeepSWE isn't the only benchmark around, either. Artificial Analysis ranks DSF-1017 (max) as only #2 on its intelligence index within the large open-weight class, with a score of 45. For reference, the most seemingly intelligent model, Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback), rings in at 58. It's one of the fastest models in its category, too, and its cost-per-task is edged out only by Xiaomi's MiMo V2.6-Pro.

This all sounds too good to be true, but everyone knows the adage of "fast, cheap, and reliable, pick two." So what's the catch? In one word: hallucination. Just because a model is smart doesn't mean it's reliable. Broadly speaking, users prefer models that don't answer when they lack supporting facts, and DSF-1017 doesn't seem very good at knowing what it doesn't know.

signals.excerpt:

Discover Summary

NVIDIA has introduced a global performance tuner in TensorRT 11.1 that automatically searches build paths for AI inference engines and compares their performance. In a comparison across 10 workloads, tuning delivered performance of 1.14–1.63x that of the default path, but the results are limited to those workloads.

...

## Automatic Search Feature Introduced in TensorRT 11.1

NVIDIA has introduced a global performance tuner in TensorRT 11.1 that automatically searches and compares multiple build paths for AI inference engines. The feature generates build paths from combinations of compiler settings, then builds an engine for each path and measures overall inference performance.

The command-line tool `trtexec` expands search conditions into individual build paths and evaluates candidate engines in sequence. Candidates that fail to build or do not meet the specified accuracy criteria are excluded, and the path with the highest measured performance among the remaining engines is selected.
